claim: The primate brain contains distinct areas densely populated by face-selective neurons.
source: The primate brain contains distinct areas densely populated by face-selective neurons.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about primate brain organization.

claim: Face-patch ML contains neurons selective for contrast relationships between face parts.
source: One of these, face-patch ML, contains neurons selective for contrast relationships between face parts.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work in the manuscript.

claim: Contrast-relationships can serve as powerful heuristics for face detection.
source: Such contrast-relationships can serve as powerful heuristics for face detection.
evidence: This is supported by citations to computational and theoretical work mentioned elsewhere in the manuscript.

claim: Inactivation of ML impairs face detection.
source: We found that inactivation of ML impairs face detection.
evidence: This is the primary experimental finding supported by behavioral data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Inactivation of areas outside ML did not affect face detection.
source: The effect was anatomically specific, as inactivation of areas outside ML did not affect face detection
evidence: This is supported by off-target injection control experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Inactivation of ML impaired face detection while sparing body and object detection.
source: it was categorically specific, as inactivation of ML impaired face detection while sparing body and object detection.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data comparing performance across different object categories.

claim: ML function is crucial for detection of faces in natural scenes.
source: These results establish that ML function is crucial for detection of faces in natural scenes, performing a critical first step on which other face processing operations can build.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented.

claim: For primates, faces are among the most behaviorally salient and socially relevant visual stimuli.
source: For primates, faces are among the most behaviorally salient and socially relevant visual stimuli (Leopold and Rhodes, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Leopold and Rhodes, 2010.

claim: The primate brain contains multiple interconnected cortical areas specialized for face processing, the face-patch network.
source: Reflecting this importance , the primate brain contains multiple interconnected cortical areas specialized for face processing, the face-patch network (Tsao et al., 2006, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Tsao et al., 2006, 2008.

claim: The middle-lateral face patch (ML) is one of the earliest nodes in the face processing hierarchy.
source: The middle-lateral face patch (ML), one of the earliest nodes in the face processing hierarchy, consists of neurons highly selective for faces (Tsao et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tsao et al., 2006 and represents established knowledge about the face-patch hierarchy.

claim: ML consists of neurons highly selective for faces.
source: The middle-lateral face patch (ML), one of the earliest nodes in the face processing hierarchy, consists of neurons highly selective for faces (Tsao et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Tsao et al., 2006.

claim: Half of ML neurons exhibit sensitivity for coarse contrast relationships between face regions such as vertical adjacency of a bright forehead region above a darker eye region.
source: Half of ML neurons exhibit sensitivity for coarse contrast relationships between face regions such as vertical adjacency of a bright forehead region above a darker eye region (Ohayon et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Ohayon et al., 2012.

claim: Qualitative contrast signatures for faces provide a computationally powerful means for face detection.
source: Such qualitative contrast signatures for faces have been shown to provide a computationally powerful means for face detection (Sinha, 2002; Viola and Jones, 2004; Gilad et al., 2009)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Sinha, 2002; Viola and Jones, 2004; Gilad et al., 2009.

claim: Face detection is the most fundamental computation for all subsequent face-processing.
source: the most fundamental computation for all subsequent face-processing (Tsao and Livingstone, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Tsao and Livingstone, 2008.

claim: Two macaques were trained on a touchscreen-based object detection task.
source: We first trained two macaques on a touchscreen-based object detection task.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure performed by the authors.

claim: Subjects were required to select an object belonging to one of three target categories – human faces, macaque bodies, or shoes.
source: From a visual scene displayed on the touchscreen, subjects were required to select an object belonging to one of three target categories – human faces, macaque bodies (socially relevant control category represented near face patches; Popivanov et al., 2012), or shoes (newly learned object category that, like faces, exhibits high within-class similarity).
evidence: This describes the experimental design and task structure.

claim: Macaque bodies are a socially relevant control category represented near face patches.
source: macaque bodies (socially relevant control category represented near face patches; Popivanov et al., 2012)
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Popivanov et al., 2012.

claim: The visual scene was composed of 24 objects at one of ten visibility levels.
source: The visual scene was composed of 24 objects, at one of ten visibility levels.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Face targets were randomly resized, rotated in-plane, and blended into a cluttered background at random locations.
source: To discourage the use of low-level features for solving the task, the face targets were randomly resized, rotated in-plane, and blended into a cluttered background at random locations (Figure 1A; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the experimental design and is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Face patch ML was localized by functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) using a standard face localizer.
source: Face patch ML was localized by functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) using a standard face localizer.
evidence: This describes the experimental method used.

claim: 5 μL (8 μL in one experiment) of muscimol (5 μg/μL) was infused to inactivate ML.
source: To inactivate ML, we stereotaxically targeted its fMRI-identified coordinates and infused 5 μL (8 μL in one experiment) of muscimol (5 μg/μL), a GABAA agonist.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Muscimol is a GABAA agonist.
source: muscimol (5 μg/μL), a GABAA agonist.
evidence: This is established pharmacological knowledge.

claim: The MR contrast agent gadolinium was co-infused with muscimol.
source: We co-infused the MR contrast agent gadolinium (Gd), the cortical spread of which closely tracks the diffusion extent of muscimol (Heiss et al., 2010; Wilke et al., 2012), as a surrogate tracer so that the extent of muscimol spread could be detected in an anatomical MR scan (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the experimental method and is supported by citations.

claim: The cortical spread of gadolinium closely tracks the diffusion extent of muscimol.
source: the cortical spread of which closely tracks the diffusion extent of muscimol (Heiss et al., 2010; Wilke et al., 2012)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Heiss et al., 2010; Wilke et al., 2012.

claim: The average volume of ML exceeding a threshold of t > 20 is approximately 58 mm3.
source: First, we determined the average volume of ML exceeding a threshold of t > 20 as ~58 mm3, corresponding to a ~5 mm-diameter sphere, consistent with published neurophysiological data (Aparicio et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a measurement from the experimental data, consistent with cited literature.

claim: The average volume of the injection at a threshold of 50% peak Gd brightness was approximately 37 mm3.
source: The average volume of the injection at a threshold of 50% peak Gd brightness was ~37 mm3, corresponding to a ~4 mm-diameter sphere.
evidence: This is a measurement from the experimental data.

claim: The theoretical maximum of volumetric ML coverage by the injection is 63.8%.
source: At the chosen thresholds, the theoretical maximum of volumetric ML coverage by the injection, assuming concentric spheres for both volumes, is 63.8%.
evidence: This is a calculation based on geometric assumptions.

claim: On average, 44% coverage of ML was achieved by the injections.
source: We achieved 44% coverage on average.
evidence: This is a measurement from the experimental data.

claim: 76% of the total injection volume was contained within the ML volume.
source: Of the total injection volume, 76% was contained within the ML volume (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a measurement from the experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Highly face-selective neurons are primarily found in the center of the face patches.
source: The high overlap of target injections with ML suggests that we silenced a large fraction of highly face-selective neurons, primarily found in the center of the face patches (Aparicio et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Aparicio et al., 2016.

claim: Off-target injections achieved 4% ML coverage with 10% of the injection contained within ML.
source: The corresponding numbers for off-target injections were 4% ML coverage with 10% of the injection contained within ML.
evidence: This is a measurement from the experimental data.

claim: The subject performed detection tasks between approximately 1 and 3 hours after muscimol injection.
source: The subject was transferred to its home cage to perform the detection tasks between ~1 and 3 hr after muscimol injection and subsequent anatomical scan, well within the time period of maximal muscimol effects (~0.5 hr to ~4 hr) (Hikosaka and Wurtz, 1985; Lomber, 1999; Dias and Segraves, 1999; Sommer and Wurtz, 2004).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure and timing.

claim: The time period of maximal muscimol effects is approximately 0.5 to 4 hours.
source: well within the time period of maximal muscimol effects (~0.5 hr to ~4 hr) (Hikosaka and Wurtz, 1985; Lomber, 1999; Dias and Segraves, 1999; Sommer and Wurtz, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Baseline performance data was gathered on Day 1, inactivation data on Day 2, and recovery data on Day 3 or 4.
source: In a typical experimental sequence, we gathered baseline performance data on Day 1, inactivation data on Day 2, and recovery data on Day 3 or 4.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Face-detection performance was reduced by approximately 11% during ML inactivation.
source: Face-detection performance was reduced by ~11% during ML inactivation (pooled over all visibilities and sessions, p<0.001, paired t-test after logit transform).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data.

claim: Performance decrements were significant for 9 out of 10 visibility levels at p<0.05.
source: Separated by visibility level, these performance decrements were significant for 9 out of 10 visibility levels at p<0.05 (FDR-corrected paired t-tests after logit transform; Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The performance reduction was well-described by a line with R2 = 0.74 and p<0.001.
source: it was well-described by a line (R2 = 0.74; p<0.001) parallel to the diagonal (slope = 0.96) with a significant negative offset (p<0.001), providing a second, visibility-independent, single-session level estimate of the performance deficit of ~15%.
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The single-session level estimate of the performance deficit is approximately 15%.
source: providing a second, visibility-independent, single-session level estimate of the performance deficit of ~15%.
evidence: This is derived from statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: Inactivation of 1 out of 12 temporal lobe face patches caused a significant and sizable reduction in face-detection performance.
source: Thus, inactivation of 1 out of 12 temporal lobe face patches (Tsao et al., 2008) caused a significant and sizable reduction in face-detection performance.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data with reference to the total number of face patches.

claim: Shift (α) was significantly higher in the inactivated conditions than during baseline (p<0.001).
source: Shift (α) and lapse rate (λ) were significantly higher in the inactivated conditions (p<0.001 and p = 0.016 respectively; paired t-test) than during baseline (red disks in Figure 2E; Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data shown in Figures 2E and 2F.

claim: Lapse rate (λ) was significantly higher in the inactivated conditions than during baseline (p = 0.016).
source: Shift (α) and lapse rate (λ) were significantly higher in the inactivated conditions (p<0.001 and p = 0.016 respectively; paired t-test) than during baseline (red disks in Figure 2E; Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data shown in Figures 2E and 2F.

claim: During inactivation, the psychometric function was shifted rightwards and asymptotically lowered.
source: In other words, during inactivation, the psychometric function was shifted rightwards and asymptotically lowered.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical results regarding shift and lapse rate.

claim: The slope of the psychometric function (β) remained unaltered by inactivation.
source: The slope of the function (β) remained unaltered by inactivation.
evidence: This is a result from the statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The average face-detection threshold increased from 0.37 ± 0.02 at baseline to 0.45 ± 0.03 during inactivation.
source: As a result, the stimulus visibility required for 50% performance (the average face-detection threshold) increased from 0.37 ± 0.02 at baseline to 0.45 ± 0.03 during the inactivation conditions.
evidence: This is a measurement derived from the experimental data.

claim: ML inactivation caused a shift of the psychometric function for face detection, but neither body nor shoe detection were significantly impaired.
source: ML inactivation caused a shift of the psychometric function for face detection, but neither body nor shoe detection were significantly impaired.
evidence: This is a result from the experimental data comparing different object categories.

claim: In recovery sessions, behavioral performance returned to baseline levels across all target categories.
source: In recovery sessions when the effect of muscimol was expected to have subsided, behavioral performance returned to baseline levels across all target categories (Figure 3B; green)
evidence: This is a result from the experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Fit parameters for performance in the recovery condition were not different from baseline for faces.
source: fit parameters for performance in the recovery condition were not different from baseline for faces (Figure 2E; Figure 2F; green) or the other target categories (not shown).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data shown in Figures 2E and 2F.

claim: The transience of the effect demonstrates that muscimol was a causative agent.
source: The transience of this effect demonstrates that muscimol was a causative agent.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the recovery data.

claim: Off-target injection volumes barely overlapped with ML (9.6%).
source: The off-target injection volumes barely overlapped with ML (9.6%; Figure 1D) or with any other face patch
evidence: This is a measurement from the experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Off-target injections resulted in only a weak and non-significant reduction in detection performance.
source: and consequently, we observed only a weak and non-significant reduction in detection performance (Figure 2E; Figure 2F; Figure 3B; blue).
evidence: This is a result from the experimental data shown in multiple figures.

claim: Only the face-inactivated condition showed significant performance deficits that were pairwise significantly different from all other category/condition combinations.
source: Only the face-inactivated condition showed significant performance deficits (F(6, 752)=17.89; p<0.0001) and threshold shifts (ANOVA; F(6, 65)=5.74; p<0.0001) that were pairwise significantly different from all of the other category/condition combinations including the body- and shoe-inactivated conditions (*p<0.05; Tukey's test).
evidence: This is a statistical result from ANCOVA and ANOVA analyses of the experimental data.

claim: The mean face-detection performance deficit was not significantly correlated with the ML-injection overlap.
source: The mean face-detection performance deficit was not significantly correlated with the ML-injection overlap (Spearman's Rho rs = 0.42; p=0.1).
evidence: This is a statistical result from correlation analysis.

claim: ML-injection overlap did not have a significant effect on the observed face-detection deficit.
source: An ANCOVA analysis with session number as independent groups and ML-injection overlap as a covariate did not reveal a significant effect of ML-injection overlap on the observed face-detection deficit (F(1,102) = 1.35; p=0.25).
evidence: This is a statistical result from ANCOVA analysis.

claim: There were no significant differences between the total number of trials the animal initiated on control or inactivation days.
source: the animal performed similar numbers of trials on control and inactivation days suggesting no change in motivation level; (2) animals performed at a high rate on high-visibility trials on all days, suggesting no distraction at the time scale of trials.
evidence: This is a result from post-hoc analysis of the behavioral data.

claim: Muscimol-induced performance deficits decreased with repeated muscimol exposure.
source: Compatible with the idea that such strategies might have been learned and used, we found muscimol-induced performance deficits to decrease with repeated muscimol exposure.
evidence: This is a result from analysis of the experimental data across sessions.

claim: There was a highly significant effect of session number on the performance deficit magnitude (F(1,752)=15.33; p<0.0001).
source: We observed a highly significant effect of session number on the performance deficit magnitude (F(1,752)=15.33; p<0.0001) with a positive slope of 0.01 ± 0.002, that is, the performance deficit caused by muscimol decreased by ~1% each session (relative to baseline performance level; Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a statistical result from ANCOVA analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The performance deficit caused by muscimol decreased by approximately 1% each session.
source: the performance deficit caused by muscimol decreased by ~1% each session (relative to baseline performance level; Figure 3E).
evidence: This is derived from statistical analysis of the experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Equivalent inactivated visibilities for faces were significantly lower than baseline visibilities (p<0.01).
source: As expected from the increased detection threshold, equivalent inactivated visibilities for faces were significantly lower than baseline visibilities (p<0.01; paired t-test).
evidence: This is a statistical result from analysis of the experimental data.

claim: Local inactivation of smaller cortical regions can cause face-processing deficits specific to the visual field they represent.
source: Previous experiments in head-fixed preparations have demonstrated that local inactivation of smaller cortical regions can cause face-processing deficits specific to the visual field they represent (e.g., Afraz et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Afraz et al., 2015.

claim: Face-patch ML shows a foveal bias.
source: As face-patch ML shows a foveal bias (Janssens et al., 2014)
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Janssens et al., 2014.

claim: The center of ML contains neurons with the strongest face selectivity.
source: and because the center of ML contains neurons with the strongest face selectivity (Aparicio et al., 2016)
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Aparicio et al., 2016.

claim: Direct cortical stimulation and suppression have been used successfully to alter face perception in humans and macaques.
source: Direct cortical stimulation and suppression have been used successfully to alter face perception in humans and macaques (Allison et al., 1994; Parvizi et al., 2012; Chong et al., 2013; Jonas et al., 2014; Afraz et al., 2006; Roy et al., 2014; Afraz et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The spread of muscimol was directly visualized and limited to the functionally defined coordinates of an fMRI-identified face area.
source: We directly visualized and limited the spread of muscimol to the functionally defined coordinates of an fMRI-identified face area.
evidence: This describes a methodological advance of the current study.

claim: Receptive fields in posterior IT are spatially specific.
source: Receptive fields in posterior IT, the region in which ML is located, are spatially specific (Kobatake and Tanaka, 1994)
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Kobatake and Tanaka, 1994.

claim: The two hemispheres cover different parts of the visual field.
source: and thus the two hemispheres cover different parts of the visual field (Rajimehr et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Rajimehr et al., 2014.

claim: Unilateral inactivation is expected to affect only part of the visual field.
source: Therefore, unilateral inactivation is expected to affect only part of the visual field (Afraz et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on cited literature about receptive field organization.

claim: Bodies are represented in the direct vicinity of ML.
source: with little or no effects on one object category, bodies, that is represented in the direct vicinity of ML (Popivanov et al., 2012)
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Popivanov et al., 2012.

claim: One male rhesus (Subject O) and one male cynomolgus (Subject I) macaque were studied.
source: We studied one male rhesus (Subject O) and one male cynomolgus (Subject I) macaque, 3.5–5 years in age and weighing between 4.5 and 9 kgs.
evidence: This describes the subjects used in the study.

claim: All MRI data was acquired on a 3T Siemens Tim Trio MRI scanner.
source: We acquired all MRI data on a 3T Siemens Tim Trio MRI scanner and used an AC88 gradient insert (Siemens) for functional scans.
evidence: This describes the equipment used in the study.

claim: A dose of Feraheme containing 8-10 mg/kg of iron was injected before each functional scan to increase functional contrast.
source: A dose of Feraheme (AMAG Pharmaceuticals) containing 8-10 mg/kg of iron was injected into a saphenous vein before each functional scan to increase functional contrast.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Stimuli for fMRI imaging consisted of grayscale pictures of rhesus macaque faces, cynomolgus macaque faces, fruits and vegetables, monkey bodies, manmade objects, and phase-scrambled versions of the fruit and vegetable pictures.
source: Stimuli consisted of grayscale pictures of rhesus macaque faces, cynomolgus macaque faces, fruits and vegetables, monkey bodies, manmade objects, and phase-scrambled versions of the fruit and vegetable pictures, presented in separate 24 s blocks.
evidence: This describes the stimuli used in the fMRI experiments.

claim: Images were matched within and across all categories for total screen area, placed on a pink noise background and normalized for luminance and frequency amplitude.
source: Images were matched within and across all categories for total screen area, placed on a pink noise background and normalized for luminance and frequency amplitude using the SHINE toolbox (http://www.mapageweb.umontreal.ca/gosselif/shine; Willenbockel et al., 2010).
evidence: This describes the stimulus preparation procedure.

claim: The contrast [(rhesus faces + cynomolgus faces) > all other object categories] was used to map the face patches.
source: To map the face patches, we used the contrast [(rhesus faces + cynomolgus faces) > all other object categories].
evidence: This describes the fMRI analysis method.

claim: Subjects were trained on a touchscreen-based object detection task.
source: We trained subjects on a touchscreen-based object detection task.
evidence: This describes the behavioral training procedure.

claim: The subject initiated the trial by touching a central disc, the color of which indicated the target category.
source: The subject initiated the trial by touching a central disc (4.3 cm dia.), the color of which indicated the target category (red-faces; blue-body parts; green-shoes).
evidence: This describes the behavioral task design.

claim: Subjects had 3 seconds to choose the correct target object.
source: Subjects had 3 s to choose the correct target object, upon which they were rewarded with a small amount of juice or water.
evidence: This describes the behavioral task parameters.

claim: Grayscale images of human faces were constructed from a multiracial face database.
source: Grayscale images of human faces were constructed from a multiracial face database (http://wiki.cnbc.cmu.edu/Face_Place, Michael Tarr).
evidence: This describes the source of behavioral stimuli.

claim: The goal of random scaling and rotation manipulations was to minimize the consistent spatial occurrence of low-level features.
source: The goal of these manipulations was to minimize the consistent spatial occurrence of low-level features and ensure that face stimuli possessed highly variable outlines.
evidence: This explains the rationale for the stimulus design.

claim: The visual texture background was introduced to disrupt normal coarse contrast relationships in faces and introduce face-like coarse contrast relationships at non-target locations.
source: The visual texture background was introduced to both disrupt the normal coarse contrast relationships in faces, and to introduce face-like coarse contrast relationships at non-target locations.
evidence: This explains the rationale for the task design.

claim: A hard time constraint of 3 seconds was imposed to obtain a psychometric function that better reflects rapid face detection in scenes.
source: We imposed a hard time constraint of 3 s, giving subjects time for about two scans of the array. Trials that would have taken longer response times (had the time constraint not been imposed) were thus converted to timeouts or misses attributable to forced guessing, allowing us to obtain a psychometric function that better reflects rapid face detection in scenes.
evidence: This explains the rationale for the task design.

claim: 11 on-target injections and 10 off-target injections were performed in three hemispheres.
source: We performed 11 on-target injections and 10 off-target injections in three hemispheres.
evidence: This describes the experimental design and sample size.

claim: Psychometric functions with three parameters (shift, slope, and lapse rate) were fit to each session's performance data.
source: To determine which behavioral parameters were affected by inactivation, psychometric functions (Equation 1 in Materials and methods; Wichmann and Hill, 2001) with three parameters – shift along the abscissa (α), slope (β), and lapse rate (λ, the difference between maximum and perfect performance) - were then fit to each session's performance data (R2 > 0.9 for face detection in all sessions).
evidence: This describes the data analysis method.

claim: R2 > 0.9 for face detection in all sessions.
source: (R2 > 0.9 for face detection in all sessions).
evidence: This is a measure of goodness of fit for the psychometric functions.

claim: Object recognition performance in monkeys does not depend on response modality.
source: Recent evidence suggests that object recognition performance in monkeys does not depend on response modality – performance measured using saccades with eye-tracking, or touch with no gaze tracking, was similar to human object recognition performance measured without eye-tracking (Rajalingham et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Rajalingham et al., 2015.
